children: Oracle reported solid first-quarter earnings results on Thursday afternoon. Its shares jumped 7% in Friday's premarket, after falling 5.4% in regular trading.

Adjusted earnings per share were $1.92, up from $1.47 last year, and ahead of Wall Street projections of $1.74. Revenue for the quarter reached $19.3 billion, above expectations of $19.1 billion and up 30% from a year ago.

Beyond the headline results, the most important number was revenue from the company's cloud infrastructure segment, which rents out AI servers over the internet. This unit represents the lion's share of the company's giant backlog, now up to $664 billion, and is the foundation of both the bull and bear cases for Oracle.
Cloud infrastructure sales rose 121% from last year to $7.4 billion, beating expectations. The rest of the company grew at only a 3% clip.
The company provided second-quarter guidance that was roughly in line with expectations. For the fiscal year, Oracle edged up its adjusted EPS and revenue guidance.

Before the artificial-intelligence investment boom, Oracle was a mature software company that grew slowly, but also kicked off a lot of free cash flow that became shareholder cash return through dividends and share repurchases, halving the share count in the process.

But Oracle's growth story is built on that backlog and cloud infrastructure taking over. Only 18% of sales in fiscal year 2025, the segment is expected to produce 60% of revenue next year and keep growing from there.
Though cloud has a lower gross margin than software, the company has been able to offset that with operating expense efficiency, and adjusted operating margin even ticked up from last year.

With the rise of cloud, Oracle has transformed its balance sheet and cash flow. Capital expenditures are rising dramatically, expected at $92 billion this fiscal year, up from $56 billion last year. That estimate may be too low; the company spent $28 billion on capex, in the first quarter alone. In fiscal year 2024, the company only spent $6.9 billion on capex. In the process, free cash flow has gone negative, and share buybacks have ended. The share count is rising.
Analysts don't expect free cash flow until 2030. To fund these investments, Oracle added $37 billion in long-term debt last year and sold $20 billion in equity during the first quarter.

Almost half of Oracle's backlog comes from a single cloud infrastructure contract with OpenAI, and, to some extent, Oracle stock has become a proxy for sentiment on the fast-growing AI start-up, which may go public soon.

This depressed Oracle's stock over the summer, as enthusiasm for OpenAI faded with the fast rise in the sales of its main competitor, Anthropic. Moreover, both companies are seeing pricing pressure from much less expensive AI models, and OpenAI lowered prices across its GPT-5.6 family of models in July and August. But September saw another shift in OpenAI sentiment, and Oracle stock is up 8.4% coming into Thursday.
Though the OpenAI partnership remains the most important for Oracle, its non-OpenAI backlog more than doubled in the past year, lessening its dependence on that one contract.
